title: CORRELATIVE CONJUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ Correlative conjunctions → pairs of words that work together to connect equal or related grammatical elements.

◆ COMMON PAIRS
both...and, either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, whether...or, rather...than, no sooner...than, hardly...when, scarcely...when.

✓ Both John and Mary passed the exam.
✓ You can either study now or study later.

⚠️ The two parts connected by a correlative conjunction should normally have the same grammatical structure.

title: BOTH...AND
notes:
✓ Both...and → connects two positive/equivalent elements and means 'the two together.'

✓ Both Sara and Hana are students.
✓ He speaks both English and Amharic.
✓ She is both intelligent and hardworking.

◆ PATTERN
both + A + and + B.

⚠️ With both...and, a plural subject normally takes a plural verb.

✓ Both the teacher and the student are ready.

❌ Both the teacher and the student is ready.

title: EITHER...OR
notes:
✓ Either...or → presents two alternatives or choices.

✓ You can either stay here or come with us.
✓ Either John or Peter will help you.
✓ You can choose either tea or coffee.

◆ PATTERN
either + A + or + B.

✓ Meaning → one choice, one possibility, or sometimes one of two alternatives.

⚠️ With two different subjects, verb agreement commonly follows the subject closest to the verb.

✓ Either the students or the teacher is responsible.
✓ Either the teacher or the students are responsible.

title: NEITHER...NOR
notes:
✓ Neither...nor → connects two negative alternatives and means 'not A and not B.'

✓ Neither John nor Peter came.
✓ She speaks neither French nor German.
✓ Neither the teacher nor the students were ready.

◆ PATTERN
neither + A + nor + B.

⚠️ Avoid another negative with neither...nor.

❌ She doesn't speak neither French nor German.
✓ She speaks neither French nor German.

✓ Neither...nor already expresses negation.

title: NOT ONLY...BUT ALSO
notes:
✓ Not only...but also → emphasizes two qualities, actions, people, or facts.

✓ She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
✓ He speaks not only English but also French.
✓ The course is not only useful but also interesting.

◆ PATTERN
not only + A + but also + B.

✓ The structure emphasizes that both statements are true, with extra emphasis on the second.

title: PARALLEL STRUCTURE
notes:
✓ Parallel structure → the elements connected by correlative conjunctions should have matching grammatical forms.

✓ She likes both reading and writing. → V-ing + V-ing.
✓ He is both intelligent and hardworking. → adjective + adjective.
✓ They will either travel by bus or travel by train. → verb phrase + verb phrase.

❌ She likes both reading and to write.
✓ She likes both reading and writing.

✓ Match noun with noun, adjective with adjective, verb form with verb form, and phrase with phrase.

title: WHETHER...OR
notes:
✓ Whether...or → presents alternatives or shows that two possibilities are being considered.

✓ I don't know whether he will come or stay.
✓ Whether you agree or disagree, we must continue.
✓ She must decide whether to study or work.

✓ Meaning → one possibility or the other, or regardless of which possibility is true.

◆ WHETHER CAN BE FOLLOWED BY
✓ whether + clause + or + clause.
✓ whether + to-infinitive + or + to-infinitive.

✓ I don't know whether to stay or leave.

title: RATHER...THAN
notes:
✓ Rather...than → expresses preference for one thing over another.

✓ I would rather walk than take a taxi.
✓ She would rather study than watch television.

◆ PATTERN
would rather + V1 + than + V1.

⚠️ Keep the verb forms parallel.

❌ I would rather walking than take a taxi.
✓ I would rather walk than take a taxi.

✓ With nouns, prefer...to is usually more natural.
✓ I prefer tea to coffee.

title: NO SOONER...THAN
notes:
✓ No sooner...than → shows that one event happened immediately after another.

✓ No sooner had I arrived than it started raining.

◆ FORMAL PATTERN
no sooner + had + subject + V3 + than + clause.

✓ Meaning → event B happened immediately after event A.

⚠️ No sooner is normally followed by than, not when.

❌ No sooner had I arrived when it started raining.
✓ No sooner had I arrived than it started raining.

title: HARDLY...WHEN
notes:
✓ Hardly...when → shows that one event happened immediately before another.

✓ Hardly had I arrived when the meeting began.

◆ FORMAL PATTERN
hardly + had + subject + V3 + when + clause.

✓ Meaning → almost immediately after.

⚠️ Hardly is normally paired with when.

❌ Hardly had I arrived than the meeting began.
✓ Hardly had I arrived when the meeting began.

title: SCARCELY...WHEN
notes:
✓ Scarcely...when → similar to hardly...when and describes two events occurring almost immediately one after another.

✓ Scarcely had she left when the phone rang.

◆ PATTERN
scarcely + had + subject + V3 + when + clause.

✓ Meaning → almost immediately after.

✓ No sooner → than.
✓ Hardly → when.
✓ Scarcely → when.

title: INVERSION WITH NO SOONER / HARDLY / SCARCELY
notes:
✓ When no sooner, hardly, or scarcely begins the sentence, subject-auxiliary inversion is normally used.

✓ Normal → I had hardly arrived when it rained.
✓ Inverted → Hardly had I arrived when it rained.

✓ Normal → She had no sooner left than he arrived.
✓ Inverted → No sooner had she left than he arrived.

✓ Structure → negative/restrictive expression + auxiliary + subject + V3.

⚠️ Do not use ordinary word order after these initial expressions in formal constructions.

❌ No sooner I had arrived than...
✓ No sooner had I arrived than...

title: SUBJECT–VERB AGREEMENT
notes:
✓ With either...or and neither...nor, when the subjects differ in number, the verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject.

✓ Either the teacher or the students are responsible.
✓ Either the students or the teacher is responsible.
✓ Neither the manager nor the workers are available.
✓ Neither the workers nor the manager is available.

✓ This is called proximity agreement.

⚠️ With both...and, use a plural verb.

✓ Both the teacher and the student are ready.

title: CORRELATIVE PAIRS WITH NOUNS
notes:
✓ Correlative conjunctions can connect nouns and noun phrases.

✓ Both the teacher and the student attended.
✓ Either the red shirt or the blue shirt is suitable.
✓ Neither the bus nor the train was available.
✓ Not only the students but also the teachers attended.

✓ Ensure both connected elements perform the same grammatical role.

title: CORRELATIVE PAIRS WITH VERBS
notes:
✓ Correlative conjunctions can connect verbs or verb phrases.

✓ She both studies and works.
✓ He either walks or takes the bus.
✓ They neither complained nor left.
✓ She not only sings but also dances.

⚠️ Keep the verb forms parallel.

❌ She both studies and working.
✓ She both studies and works.

title: CORRELATIVE PAIRS WITH ADJECTIVES
notes:
✓ Correlative conjunctions can connect adjectives describing the same subject.

✓ The exam was both difficult and interesting.
✓ She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
✓ The solution is either simple or complicated.

✓ Pattern → subject + linking verb + paired adjectives.

⚠️ Keep adjective forms parallel.

title: CORRELATIVE PAIRS WITH CLAUSES
notes:
✓ Correlative conjunctions can connect complete or nearly complete clauses.

✓ Either you apologize or you leave.
✓ Whether he comes or stays, we will continue.
✓ Not only did she pass the exam, but she also won a prize.

✓ When full clauses are connected, check tense, subject, word order, and parallel structure.

title: NOT ONLY...BUT ALSO + INVERSION
notes:
✓ When not only begins a sentence and introduces an emphatic clause, inversion may be required.

✓ Not only did she pass the exam, but she also won a prize.

◆ PATTERN
Not only + auxiliary + subject + verb...

✓ Not only is he intelligent, but he is also hardworking.

⚠️ If not only is placed in the normal middle position, inversion is usually unnecessary.

✓ She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.

title: COMMON ERRORS
notes:
❌ Both John as Mary came.
✓ Both John and Mary came.

❌ Either tea and coffee.
✓ Either tea or coffee.

❌ Neither John or Peter came.
✓ Neither John nor Peter came.

❌ Not only intelligent but also hardworking. → incomplete if used as a full paired structure without context.
✓ She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.

❌ No sooner had he arrived when she left.
✓ No sooner had he arrived than she left.

❌ Hardly had I arrived than it started.
✓ Hardly had I arrived when it started.

❌ She likes both reading and to write.
✓ She likes both reading and writing.

❌ He would rather walking than drive.
✓ He would rather walk than drive.

title: CORRELATIVE CONJUNCTION MASTER TABLE
notes:
◆ BOTH...AND → two positive elements.
✓ Both A and B.

◆ EITHER...OR → alternatives/choices.
✓ Either A or B.

◆ NEITHER...NOR → two negative alternatives.
✓ Neither A nor B.

◆ NOT ONLY...BUT ALSO → two elements with emphasis.
✓ Not only A but also B.

◆ WHETHER...OR → alternatives/possibilities.
✓ Whether A or B.

◆ RATHER...THAN → preference.
✓ Rather A than B / would rather A than B.

◆ NO SOONER...THAN → one event immediately follows another.
✓ No sooner had A happened than B happened.

◆ HARDLY...WHEN → almost immediate sequence.
✓ Hardly had A happened when B happened.

◆ SCARCELY...WHEN → almost immediate sequence.
✓ Scarcely had A happened when B happened.

title: EXAM GUIDE
notes:
◆ 1. Identify the two ideas being connected.

◆ 2. Choose the pair according to meaning.

◆ 3. Check parallel structure.

◆ 4. Check subject–verb agreement with either...or and neither...nor.

◆ 5. Remember the fixed pairs:
→ both + and
→ either + or
→ neither + nor
→ not only + but also
→ whether + or
→ no sooner + than
→ hardly + when
→ scarcely + when

◆ 6. Check inversion after initial no sooner, hardly, scarcely, and emphatic not only.

◆ 7. Avoid unnecessary double negatives.

◆ QUICK MEMORY
BOTH → AND
EITHER → OR
NEITHER → NOR
NOT ONLY → BUT ALSO
WHETHER → OR
NO SOONER → THAN
HARDLY → WHEN
SCARCELY → WHEN

✓ Golden rule → Correlative conjunctions work as pairs, so both sides must be grammatically balanced and the correct pair must be used.
